explanations.explanation: Baal is it. Hosea 13:1 says Ephraim was exalted in Israel, “But he incurred guilt through Baal, and he died.” When Ephraim spoke, people trembled, and that still didn't protect him. I think that's a sobering turn, so I'm not going to joke on it.

Dagon was the god of the Philistines (Judges 16:23), so it's a real idol name, just not the one in this verse. Hosea 13:1 says Ephraim “…incurred guilt through Baal, and he died.” Idol names pile up like old receipts in a junk drawer, so mixing them up is easy to do.

Molech was a false god too (Leviticus 18:21), but he isn't the name in this verse. Hosea 13:1 says Ephraim “…incurred guilt through Baal, and he died.” So the name to hold onto here is Baal. Molech just wandered in from another page.

True. Hosea 13:2 says the idols are made skillfully from their silver, “all of them the work of craftsmen.” So these weren't rough lumps of metal. A lot of careful work went into them, and that makes them the exact opposite of a good idea.

The text says the opposite. Hosea 13:2 calls the idols “skillfully made from their silver, all of them the work of craftsmen.” So real craftsmen did the work. I'd say talent was never the problem here.

They vanish. Morning mist, early dew, chaff blown from a threshing floor, and smoke through an open window are all gone before you can grab them (Hosea 13:3). The LORD says that's what the idol makers will be like. Four pictures, one message, and nobody can say it didn't get through.

Not one of the four grows stronger. Hosea 13:3 says the people will be like the morning mist, the early dew “that vanishes,” chaff blown away, and smoke through an open window. All four are things that disappear. Nobody wants to be compared to smoke on its way out.

None of these stay put. Hosea 13:3 uses dew “that vanishes,” chaff blown from a threshing floor, and smoke going out an open window. All of them are things that move on and are gone. Mist doesn't wait around either.
Wilderness. The LORD says, “I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought.” (Hosea 13:5) He was in the picture long before they had pasture. Dry land, and He was already there.
A palace sounds comfy, but the LORD doesn't say it. Hosea 13:5 says, “I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought.” That's a dry, hard place, nothing like a palace. No red carpet anywhere.

A vineyard would be a lovely place to be known, but it isn't what the verse says. The LORD says, “I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought.” (Hosea 13:5) A land of drought is about as far from a vineyard as you can get.

They forget the LORD. Hosea 13:6 says, “When they had pasture, they became satisfied; when they were satisfied, their hearts became proud, and as a result they forgot Me.” Look at the steps in that verse: pasture, satisfied, proud, forgot. Full bellies can make the heart drift.
No temple gets built in this verse. Hosea 13:6 says their hearts became proud, “and as a result they forgot Me.” The result is forgetting, not building. The verse is about where their hearts went.

Egypt only shows up in verse 4, where the LORD says He has been their God ever since the land of Egypt. Nobody goes back there in verse 6. Hosea 13:6 says their hearts became proud, “and as a result they forgot Me.” The trouble here is in the heart, not on a map.

A bear. The LORD says, “Like a bear robbed of her cubs I will attack them.” (Hosea 13:8) That makes three animals so far: lion, leopard and bear. This is a stern warning, and I'll leave the animals to say it.
No wolf here. Hosea 13:8 says, “Like a bear robbed of her cubs I will attack them.” The animals in these verses are a lion, a leopard, a bear and a wild beast. The wolf didn't make the list.

The fox doesn't show up in these verses. Hosea 13:8 says, “Like a bear robbed of her cubs I will attack them.” The animals named are a lion, a leopard and a bear, plus a wild beast tearing. A fox would've been a much smaller problem.

The LORD says, “You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me,” and then names Himself as their helper (Hosea 13:9). So the trouble is that they stood against the One who was helping them. I think that's a hard thing to hear. Look at who He calls Himself even then.

explanations.answer: Their king lost a great battle
explanations.explanation: A lost battle isn't the reason given. In Hosea 13:9 the LORD says, “…because you are against Me,” and He calls Himself their helper. Verse 10 does ask where their king is, but it never says he lost a battle. The text puts it on their standing against Him.

The neighbors don't come up in this verse at all. Hosea 13:9 gives the reason: “…because you are against Me,” and He calls Himself their helper. I won't add a reason the text doesn't give. This one is about Israel and the LORD.

The text says something very different. Hosea 13:11 says, “So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away.” A reward would come with a smile, and this didn't. The king came in anger.

False. Hosea 13:11 says, “So in My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away.” He gave the king in anger, not as a reward. The people had said, “Give me a king and princes” (Hosea 13:10), and I'd call that a request to think twice about.

explanations.answer: He fails to present himself at birth
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Labor pains come, “but he is an unwise son. When the time arrives, he fails to present himself at the opening of the womb.” (Hosea 13:13) It's a picture of an unwise son who doesn't show up when the time comes. Ouch.

explanations.answer: He is born into a king's house
explanations.explanation: No king's house in this verse. Hosea 13:13 says that when the time arrives, the unwise son “fails to present himself at the opening of the womb.” The picture is about what Ephraim doesn't do. Palaces aren't in it.

explanations.answer: He is born holding his brother's heel
explanations.explanation: That's Jacob, Isaac's son, who was born holding his brother Esau's heel (Genesis 25:26). It's a different story. In Hosea 13:13, the unwise son “fails to present himself at the opening of the womb.” Two birth pictures, and only one is on this card.

explanations.answer: Ransom from the power of Sheol
explanations.explanation: Yes, a promise right in the middle of the warnings. The LORD says, “I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death.” (Hosea 13:14) Sheol is the place of the dead. That's a big promise, so hold onto it.

explanations.answer: A new king for the land
explanations.explanation: A new king isn't the promise here. Verses 10 and 11 talk about the king they asked for, but verse 14 turns to something else. The LORD says, “I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death.” (Hosea 13:14) The promise is about rescue from Sheol.

There's no covenant with Death in this verse. The LORD says, “I will ransom them from the power of Sheol; I will redeem them from Death.” (Hosea 13:14) He promises to ransom and redeem, and He doesn't make a deal with Death. I think that's a good bit of news.
The LORD. Hosea 13:15 says, “an east wind will come—a wind from the LORD rising up from the desert.” This wind doesn't just happen by chance. It comes from Him.
Baal is the name from verse 1, but he isn't sending this wind. Hosea 13:15 says it is “a wind from the LORD rising up from the desert.” It comes from the LORD, so Baal can't take credit for it.

The king can't send a wind, and the text doesn't say he does. Hosea 13:15 says it is “a wind from the LORD rising up from the desert.” Verse 10 asked where the king was to save them. I'd say nobody is checking his schedule for this one.
True. Hosea 13:15 says, “His fountain will fail, and his spring will run dry.” The east wind dries up the water. Ephraim can flourish all he wants, but the LORD says this wind is coming.

The text says it will. Hosea 13:15 says, “His fountain will fail, and his spring will run dry.” Ephraim may flourish among his brothers, but the east wind changes that. The spring is the one thing that doesn't hold up.
His treasury. Hosea 13:15 says, “The wind will plunder his treasury of every precious article.” Every precious article, not just a few. That's a whole lot of emptying.
Grain isn't mentioned here. Hosea 13:15 says, “The wind will plunder his treasury of every precious article.” So it's the treasury that gets emptied. The text doesn't mention his fields.

The sheep are safe in this verse, because the text doesn't mention them at all. Hosea 13:15 says, “The wind will plunder his treasury of every precious article.” It's the treasury that gets plundered. The flocks aren't on the list.

That's the reason given. Hosea 13:16 says, “Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God.” The verse that follows is very heavy, so I'll just say this part plainly. The text gives the reason and I'll keep to it.

Tribute isn't mentioned in this verse. Hosea 13:16 says, “Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God.” The reason the text gives is rebellion against her God. I won't add another.

The prophets aren't mentioned in this verse. Hosea 13:16 says, “Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God.” That is the reason the text gives. I'd rather stick to what it says than guess at more.
